stills.heading: The Harmonic Vocal Quartet
stills.caption: Lesson 6 · Harmony Course · Storm Studios Learning
stills.narration: Hello, and welcome back to Storm Studios Learning. In the previous lesson we completed the ideas of degrees, chords and tonality. Today we take a very important step: we are going to write chords for the harmonic vocal quartet.

stills.heading: Individual chords
stills.caption: No melodic motion or connections yet
stills.narration: In this lesson we will build individual chords. We will not yet see how each voice moves from one chord to the next, or how chords are connected. We will study that later.

stills.heading: Soprano · alto · tenor · bass
stills.caption: Two female and two male voices
stills.narration: The vocal quartet has two female voices, soprano and alto, and two male voices, tenor and bass.

stills.heading: In the original course
stills.caption: Piano score: two voices per staff, with opposite stems
stills.narration: In the original course we wrote the four voices on a piano score. Soprano and alto shared the treble clef staff, with their stems pointing in opposite directions. Tenor and bass shared the bass clef staff, also with opposite stems.

stills.heading: SATB quartet
stills.caption: One staff per voice in the sequencer
stills.narration: In the Storm Studios sequencer, in SATB quartet mode, each voice has its own staff. Soprano and alto in treble clef, tenor and bass in bass clef.

stills.heading: Ranges
stills.caption: Lowest and highest note of each voice · C4 = middle C
stills.narration: The first thing we need to know is the range of each voice. Ranges vary a lot depending on the style, the composer and the choir, but in this course we will use fixed ranges. We take C four as middle C on the piano.

stills.heading: Soprano
stills.caption: C4 to G5
stills.narration: The soprano sings from C four up to G five.

stills.heading: Alto
stills.caption: G3 to D5
stills.narration: The alto, from G three up to D five.

stills.heading: Tenor
stills.caption: B2 to G4
stills.narration: The tenor, from B two up to G four.

stills.heading: Bass
stills.caption: F2 to B3
stills.narration: And the bass, from F two up to B three.

stills.heading: Stay within these limits
stills.narration: The notes you write for each voice must stay within these limits.

stills.heading: Spacing between adjacent voices
stills.caption: Soprano–alto · alto–tenor · tenor–bass
stills.narration: The second thing is the spacing between the voices.

stills.heading: Soprano – alto
stills.caption: At most a twelfth
stills.narration: Between soprano and alto we use no more than a twelfth.

stills.heading: Alto – tenor
stills.caption: At most a tenth
stills.narration: Between alto and tenor, no more than a tenth.

stills.heading: Tenor – bass
stills.caption: At most a fifteenth: two octaves
stills.narration: And between tenor and bass, no more than a fifteenth, that is, two octaves.

stills.heading: Compact upper voices
stills.caption: A more distant bass makes the chord more robust
stills.narration: We want the three upper voices as compact as possible. On the other hand, the further the bass is from the rest, the more robust the chord sounds. The low note generates more overtones, and the other chord tones settle on them.

stills.heading: Voices do not cross
stills.caption: Soprano above alto, alto above tenor, tenor above bass
stills.narration: Also, the voices do not cross. The soprano always stays above the alto, the alto above the tenor, and the tenor above the bass.

stills.heading: Three notes, four voices
stills.caption: We double one of them
stills.narration: Now, a fifth chord has three notes: root, third and fifth. But the quartet has four voices. What do we do with three notes to make a four note chord? We double one of them.

stills.heading: C major
stills.narration: Let's look at a C major chord.

stills.heading: Bass: C3
stills.narration: In the bass we write C three.

stills.heading: Tenor: G3
stills.narration: In the tenor, G three.

stills.heading: Alto: E4
stills.narration: In the alto, E four.

stills.heading: Soprano: C5
stills.narration: And in the soprano, C again, on C five.

stills.heading: Doubled root
stills.narration: We are doubling the root.

stills.heading: Correct ranges and spacing
stills.caption: Bass–tenor 5th · tenor–alto 6th · alto–soprano 6th
stills.narration: Between bass and tenor there is a fifth, between tenor and alto a sixth, and between alto and soprano another sixth. The ranges and the spacing are correct.

stills.heading: C major
stills.narration: Let's listen to it.

stills.heading: We double any note except the leading tone
stills.caption: The only note we never double
stills.narration: We can double any note of the chord, with one exception: the leading tone. The leading tone is the only note we never double.

stills.heading: In C major, the leading tone is B
stills.caption: The seventh degree of the scale
stills.narration: In the major scale, the leading tone is the seventh degree. In C major it is B.

stills.heading: V · VII · III
stills.caption: B goes in a single voice
stills.narration: The note B appears in three chords of C major: it is the third of the fifth degree, the root of the seventh and the fifth of the third. In those three chords, B goes in a single voice.

stills.heading: The leading tone resolves to the tonic
stills.caption: Doubled, that resolution would be in two voices
stills.narration: The leading tone tends to resolve to the tonic; if we double it, that resolution ends up in two voices at once.

stills.heading: Major and minor chords
stills.caption: Preferably a doubled root or fifth
stills.narration: In major and minor chords, we preferably double the root or the fifth.

stills.heading: Doubled third
stills.caption: Possible, but a little harsh
stills.narration: Doubling the third is possible, but it sounds a little harsh.

stills.heading: Without the fifth
stills.caption: Root and third doubled
stills.narration: In major and minor chords we can also omit the fifth. Then we double the root and the third.

stills.heading: Tripled root
stills.caption: And a single third
stills.narration: Or we triple the root and use a single third.

stills.heading: Tripled third
stills.caption: Less often
stills.narration: Less often, we can triple the third.

stills.heading: We never omit the root or the third
stills.caption: Without the root the chord is not recognized · without the third we cannot tell major from minor
stills.narration: What we never omit is the root or the third. Without the root, the chord cannot be recognized. And without the third, we cannot tell whether the chord is major or minor.

stills.heading: Diminished and augmented chords
stills.caption: Always complete
stills.narration: Diminished and augmented chords are always complete.

stills.heading: VII of C major: B · D · F
stills.caption: B is the leading tone: we double D or F
stills.narration: In C major, the diminished chord is the one on the seventh degree: B, D and F. Its root, B, is the leading tone, so we double D or F.

stills.heading: III of A harmonic minor
stills.caption: C · E · G♯
stills.narration: The augmented chord appears in the harmonic minor scale, on the third degree. In A harmonic minor it is C, E and G sharp.

stills.heading: G♯ is the leading tone
stills.caption: We double C or E
stills.narration: Its fifth, G sharp, is the leading tone, so we double C or E.

stills.heading: Chord states
stills.caption: They depend on the bass note
stills.narration: Let's move on to the states of the chord. The state depends on the note in the bass.

stills.heading: Root position
stills.caption: Root in the bass
stills.narration: If the bass has the root, the chord is in root position.

stills.heading: First inversion
stills.caption: Third in the bass
stills.narration: If the bass has the third, it is in first inversion.

stills.heading: Second inversion
stills.caption: Fifth in the bass
stills.narration: And if the bass has the fifth, it is in second inversion.

stills.heading: Figures 6/3 and 6/4
stills.caption: Intervals of the other notes above the bass
stills.narration: We figure first inversion as six three, and second inversion as six four. These figures come from the intervals the other chord tones form above the bass.

stills.heading: A major in first inversion
stills.caption: A · C♯ · E
stills.narration: Let's see an example with A major in first inversion. A major is A, C sharp and E.

stills.heading: C♯ in the bass
stills.narration: To put it in first inversion, we write C sharp in the bass.

stills.heading: We do not omit the root
stills.narration: We cannot omit the root, so we write A.

stills.heading: Doubled root
stills.narration: And here we double the root.

stills.heading: G♭ major in second inversion
stills.caption: G♭ · B♭ · D♭
stills.narration: Now G flat major in second inversion. G flat major is G flat, B flat and D flat.

stills.heading: D♭ in the bass
stills.narration: For second inversion we need D flat in the bass.

stills.heading: Root and third
stills.narration: We need the root and the third.

stills.heading: Doubled fifth
stills.narration: And now we double the fifth.

stills.heading: The three states
stills.caption: C major: root position · 6/3 · 6/4
stills.narration: Let's listen to the three states.

stills.heading: Melodic position
stills.caption: It depends on the soprano note
stills.narration: Now the melodic position. The melodic position depends on the note the soprano sings.

stills.heading: Melodic position of the octave
stills.caption: Root in the soprano
stills.narration: If the soprano has the root, we say the chord is in melodic position of the octave.

stills.heading: Melodic position of the third
stills.caption: Third in the soprano
stills.narration: If it has the third, in melodic position of the third.

stills.heading: Melodic position of the fifth
stills.caption: Fifth in the soprano
stills.narration: And if it has the fifth, in melodic position of the fifth.

stills.heading: The three melodic positions
stills.narration: Let's listen to the three positions.

stills.heading: Internal spacing
stills.caption: Only the three upper voices
stills.narration: Finally, the internal spacing. Here we only look at the three upper voices: soprano, alto and tenor.

stills.heading: Close or open
stills.caption: Does another chord tone fit between them?
stills.narration: The spacing is close when no other note of the same chord fits between them. And it is open when one does fit.

stills.heading: Close spacing
stills.caption: G · C · E: no other note of C major fits
stills.narration: In this C major chord, between tenor and alto, and between alto and soprano, no other note of C major fits. The spacing is close.

stills.heading: Open spacing
stills.caption: A C fits between G and E
stills.narration: In this other one, a C fits between tenor and alto. The spacing is open.

stills.heading: Close and open
stills.narration: Let's listen to the difference.

stills.heading: Assignment for the Virtual Teacher
stills.narration: Now the assignment for the Virtual Teacher.

stills.heading: Seven chords, one per degree
stills.caption: Any major key, in any order
stills.narration: You are going to write seven chords, one on each degree of a major scale. You can choose any major key you like. And you can write the seven chords in any order you like.

stills.heading: Free state, position and spacing
stills.caption: Vary them to practice every combination
stills.narration: Each chord can have the state, melodic position and spacing you choose. I recommend varying them, so you practice every combination.

stills.heading: One whole note per measure
stills.caption: Sequencer in SATB quartet mode · export the MIDI
stills.narration: Write each chord as a whole note, with the four voices together, one chord per measure. Work in the sequencer in SATB quartet mode and export your assignment as a MIDI file.

stills.heading: The Virtual Teacher checks
stills.caption: Key and degrees · ranges · spacing and crossings · doublings, omissions and leading tone · spelling
stills.narration: The Virtual Teacher recognizes the key and the degree of each chord, and checks that all seven degrees are there. It also checks the ranges, the spacing between the voices and that they do not cross. It checks doublings, triplings and omissions, and that you have not doubled the leading tone. And it checks that the notes are spelled correctly in the key.

stills.heading: And describes each chord
stills.caption: State · melodic position · spacing
stills.narration: Also, for each chord it tells you its state, its melodic position and its spacing.

stills.heading: Let's recap
stills.narration: Let's recap.

stills.heading: Ranges and spacing
stills.caption: No voice crossing
stills.narration: The vocal quartet has four voices, each with its own range. The voices respect their spacing and do not cross.

stills.heading: Doublings and omissions
stills.caption: Never the leading tone · in major and minor chords the fifth may be omitted
stills.narration: We can double any note except the leading tone, and in major and minor chords we can omit the fifth.

stills.heading: Bass: state · soprano: melodic position
stills.caption: Three upper voices: spacing
stills.narration: The bass determines the state of the chord, the soprano its melodic position, and the three upper voices its spacing.

stills.heading: Next lessons
stills.caption: Connecting chords
stills.narration: In the following lessons we will learn to connect chords.

stills.heading: Thank you
stills.caption: See you in lesson 7
stills.narration: Thank you for joining me. See you in lesson seven.
